newsitem.title: USA: NASA calls shuttle Columbia home early.
newsitem.headline: NASA calls shuttle Columbia home early.

text.p: Mission control on Sunday ordered shuttle Columbia to cut short its 16-day science mission and return to Earth because one of its three power generators was malfunctioning and could become unsafe.
Columbia, which blasted off from Florida on Friday, was to land at the Kennedy Space Centre on Tuesday afternoon at 2:35 p.m. EDT (1835 GMT).
"We have come to the conclusion that the conservative thing to do is to land on Tuesday," shuttle director Tommy Holloway told a news conference.
The performance of the $5 million, electricity generating, fuel cell had been degrading since the shuttle's launch. It had also briefly shown signs of trouble before blastoff.
"We really do not have enough data to really understand the situation," Holloway said.

It was only the third time since shuttle missions began in 1981 that NASA has ended a mission early. A faulty fuel cell was to blame for cutting short NASA's second shuttle flight in November 1981 and a failed navigation device ended a 1991 mission prematurely.
NASA officials feared the balky power generator could spark a fire or explosion. The device would probably be shut down later on Sunday.
The shuttle is equipped with three fuel cells and could land safely on two. "We have a great deal of confidence in the two fuel cells that are operating," Holloway said.
The devices, located in the shuttle's fuselage, provide all of the shuttle's electrical power. They generate electricity by combining supercold liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen.
Weather conditions looked promising for the landing in Florida on Tuesday. The shuttle's backup landing strip in California would also be available if necessary.

Columbia's crew of seven were less than two days into a 16-day microgravity research mission. They were to light dozens of fires to study the behaviour of flame in zero gravity and grow protein crystals for medical research.
"That's certainly a disappointment," mission commander Jim Halsell said after mission control informed the crew they would have to return home early.
The astronauts had barely set up their experiments and had accomplished only a tiny fraction of their work, mission scientists said.
Once the fuel cell is shut down the laboratory work will be severely curtailed.
"We'll continue to operate as long as possible," Teresa Vanhooser, mission manager, said. "The mood is disappointment more than anything. I don't think anyone is ready to jump off a building."
The scientists were hopeful the mission, which was three years in planning, would be flown again, particularly because of expected delays in NASA's space station programme.
